title: PCA: The Math Behind the Magic 🧮
description: Eigenvectors, covariance matrices, and the core idea of finding directions of maximum variance — explained simply.

slides.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 🧭
slides.content:
# The Most Popular Dimensionality Reduction

PCA transforms data into a new coordinate system. The first axis (principal component) captures the direction of **maximum variance**; the second axis, orthogonal to the first, captures the next highest variance, etc.

Analogy: You have a scattered cloud of points in 3D. You rotate your view to find the angle that spreads the points out the most, then the next most, and so on. PCA does this mathematically.

slides.title: The Covariance Matrix 📊
slides.content:
# Measuring Relationships

Given a dataset X (n samples × p features, centered to zero mean), the covariance matrix is:
```
C = (1/(n-1)) Xᵀ X    [or (1/n) Xᵀ X]
```
- Diagonal: variances of each feature.
- Off‑diagonal: covariances between features.

C captures how features vary together. PCA finds directions where the data varies most, i.e., the eigenvectors of C.

slides.title: Eigenvectors & Eigenvalues 🧠
slides.content:
# The Key Math

For the covariance matrix C, we solve:
```
C v = λ v
```
- **v** are eigenvectors (principal components directions).
- **λ** are eigenvalues (amount of variance captured by each direction).

We sort eigenvectors by descending λ. The first k eigenvectors form a projection matrix W. We transform data:
```
Z = X W
```
Now Z has k columns (principal components), uncorrelated, ordered by variance.

**Important**: PCA assumes linear relationships and works best on scaled data.

quizData.question: What does an eigenvalue in PCA represent?

options.text: The direction of the principal component
The amount of variance explained by its corresponding eigenvector

quizData.explanation: Eigenvalues quantify variance along each principal component direction.

slides.title: Choosing How Many Components? 🔢
slides.content:
# Explained Variance Ratio

The **explained variance ratio** of component j is:
```
λⱼ / Σ λᵢ
```
This tells us the proportion of total variance captured. We typically choose k such that the cumulative explained variance reaches a threshold, e.g., 95%.

A scree plot (bar chart of λ) helps visualise the drop. The “elbow” indicates where adding more components adds little variance.

slides.title: Remember 📌
slides.content:
## PCA = Linear Transformation
PCA doesn't change the underlying data structure; it just rotates and projects. It’s a linear method — if your data lies on a curved manifold, non‑linear techniques (like kernel PCA or autoencoders) may be better.
